explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. John 12:2 says Lazarus was among those reclining at the table with Jesus. This is the man Jesus had raised from the dead, and now he's just sitting there at dinner like it's any other night. I think that's the best seat in the house.

Not quite, friend. John 12:2 says Lazarus was among those reclining at the table with Jesus. Martha was the one serving, but Lazarus had a seat and a plate. Raised from the dead and still gets to sit down for dinner, that's a good deal.
That's right, baker. Mary anointed Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair (John 12:3). Feet! Not a dab on the forehead, not a quick splash on the hands. She went low and she went all in.

Close, friend, but the text says feet. Mary anointed Jesus' feet and then wiped them with her hair (John 12:3). I'd have grabbed the hands too, so don't feel bad. I'm the guy who uses a mustache for hands.
Not shoulders, baker. John 12:3 says Mary anointed Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair. It's a small detail, but it's right there in the verse. Shoulders would be a whole different dinner.
Yes, baker. John 12:4 says Judas Iscariot was going to betray Jesus. The writer tells us that right as Judas opens his mouth. So when the question comes out, we already know who is asking.

Good guess, friend, but that's a different disciple. Denying Jesus is what Peter, one of the twelve disciples, did later (Luke 22:61). John 12:4 says Judas Iscariot was going to betray Him. Easy to mix up two men in one group chat.
Doubt is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the word here. John 12:4 says Judas Iscariot was going to betray Jesus. The writer says it plainly, before Judas even finishes his question.

Right, baker. Judas asks why the perfume wasn't sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor (John 12:5). On the surface, it sounds like a caring question. But the next verse tells us what was really going on.

No, friend. The priests aren't in Judas' question at all. He says the money should have been given to the poor (John 12:5). The priests don't show up until later in this passage, and they're not planning anything kind.

I see why you'd go there, baker, but that's not what Judas says. He says the money should have been given to the poor (John 12:5). He doesn't name himself or the other disciples. Sounds noble, doesn't it? Hold that thought.

That's right, baker. John 12:6 says Judas didn't say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief. The question sounded nice, but the writer tells us what was underneath it. A nice sentence can hide a lot.
Not a spy, friend. John 12:6 says Judas was a thief. The verse puts it plainly: he didn't care about the poor, he was a thief. No trench coat needed.

I can see why you'd guess that, baker, but the word is thief. John 12:6 says Judas did not say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief. That's the reason the writer gives, and I'll stick with his word.

Yes, baker. John 12:6 says Judas was the keeper of the money bag, and he used to take from what was put into it. Out of everything the group could have trusted him with, that's the job he had. A thief watching the cash, that's a problem.
Not the door, friend. John 12:6 says Judas was the keeper of the money bag. That job matters for his question about selling the perfume. Money was right in his hands.
Nope, baker, no mail route for Judas. John 12:6 says he was the keeper of the money bag. That's why a perfume worth three hundred denarii got his attention.

explanations.answer: He tells Judas to leave her alone
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Jesus replies, "Leave her alone…" (John 12:7). He doesn't scold Mary or argue with the numbers. He just steps in and speaks up for her.

explanations.answer: He tells Mary to sell what's left
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Jesus never tells Mary to sell anything. He says, "Leave her alone…" (John 12:7). He's talking to Judas, and He's speaking up for Mary.

explanations.answer: He tells Judas to go help the poor
explanations.explanation: I see where you're going, baker, but that's not what Jesus says. He answers with, "Leave her alone…" (John 12:7). Nothing in this passage has Him sending Judas off to help anyone.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "She has kept this perfume in preparation for the day of My burial." (John 12:7). That's a heavy word, and Jesus says it plainly. Mary's gift, in His words, is tied to that day.
I get it, baker. Perfume and a dinner, you think party. But Jesus says the day of His burial (John 12:7). It's a heavier word than wedding, and He says it plainly.
Not crowning, friend. Jesus says Mary kept the perfume in preparation for the day of His burial (John 12:7). It's a serious word, and I think this one hurts a little. Jesus says it anyway.
Not quite, baker. Jesus says, "The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me." (John 12:8). The second half goes the other way. He says they will not always have Him.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me." (John 12:8). The first part is true, but the second part flips it. They will not always have Him.

Yes, baker. The crowd came not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom He had raised from the dead (John 12:9). Picture it. The man is just trying to eat dinner and people are lining up to look at him. I'd be hiding in the pantry.

Good thought, friend, but Martha isn't who they came to see. John 12:9 says they came to see Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. Martha was busy serving, so she was probably too busy to notice a crowd.

Mary did something remarkable at that dinner, baker, but the crowd came for someone else. John 12:9 says they came to see Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. They came because of Jesus and because of Lazarus.
Right, baker, and it's a heavy one. John 12:10 says the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well. I think this is a hard verse to read, so I'll just say it plainly. They wanted him dead.
It's a heavier plan than that, friend. John 12:10 says the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus. Arrest isn't the word the text gives. I think this part is hard to hear.

explanations.answer: Put him out of the synagogue
explanations.explanation: That's a different story, baker. People being put out of the synagogue comes up in John 9:22. Here, John 12:10 says the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus. It's a heavy verse, and the text says it straight.

That's right, baker. John 12:11 says that on account of Lazarus, many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus. That's the reason the text gives for the chief priests' plan. Lazarus was a living sign of what Jesus had done.

Not false, friend. John 12:11 says that on account of Lazarus, many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus. That's the reason the text gives. The plan against Lazarus is tied to people believing in Jesus.
